subtype: Approach: using platform reporting and official complaint routes [Action]
passage: Nadia's father Gabriel set the laptop on the kitchen table in Montreal, with Nadia sitting beside him. First they used the report button on the app to ask for the images to be taken down, and screenshotted the confirmation. Then Gabriel filled in the online form on the official police cybercrime site while Nadia's mother read out the dates and names from the list. On Monday they met the school's safety lead, who said the school has a written policy, that staff would deal with the group chat, and that sharing pictures of a young person is treated as a serious matter. Nobody, the lead said, should forward the pictures, even to warn others. Nadia said very little, but she didn't leave the room.

qa.q: Where did Gabriel file the complaint?
qa.a: On the official police cybercrime site.

qa.q: What might Nadia have been feeling at the kitchen table?
qa.a: Anxious and exposed, but supported: she said very little, yet stayed in the room with her parents.

qa.q: What else could the family do, and why?
qa.a: Ask the school counsellor to check in with Nadia, since practical reports help but Nadia also needs emotional support.

qa.q: How does the evening look to Gabriel?
qa.a: Gabriel is probably angry and protective, and filling in forms gives him a concrete way to help his daughter.

grounding: A family reports images to the app, files an official complaint and the school follows its safety policy.

passage:
The counsellor's office was quiet except for the ceiling fan. Tushar sat between both parents while Ms Nandini, the school counsellor, read the printouts: photos someone had secretly taken of Tushar in the swimming-pool changing room, now passing between phones.
“Here is what happens now,” she said. “This is serious, and the school's safety policy starts today. The principal is informed, and the students involved will be spoken to with their parents.”
Tushar's father already had the app open. “We reported every post for removal this morning. Two are down.”
“Good. Keep the report numbers,” Ms Nandini said. “And because images like these of a student are a serious offence, the complaint should also go through the cybercrime portal. Would you like to file it here, now, with me?”
They did, at her computer, attaching the screenshots. Tushar watched the confirmation number appear and let out a breath held all week.

qa.q: How many reported posts were already down?
What does Tushar letting out a long breath suggest?
qa.a: It suggests relief after a week of fear and tension, now that something official had finally been done.

qa.q: Why use the app, the portal and the school instead of just one route?
qa.a: Each does a different job: the app removes posts, the complaint creates an official record, and the school deals with the students involved.

qa.q: How does the meeting look to Ms Nandini?
qa.a: Ms Nandini sees a family that has already acted, and makes sure the school's policy and the official complaint follow the same day.

grounding: Shows a family reporting images for removal, filing a cybercrime complaint, and the school starting its safety policy, since such images of a student are an offence.

passage:
Dear Tarun,
You asked why I went quiet last week, so here is the whole thing, because I'd rather you hear it from me.
Someone made a fake picture, my face pasted onto an embarrassing photo, and it went round a group on a chat app. A classmate showed it to me on Monday. I felt sick.
I told Ma that evening. She didn't panic, or if she did, she hid it. That same night she and Baba reported every post to the app using its removal form, and they filed a complaint on the cybercrime portal, with me reading out the dates. On Tuesday they came to school with me. The principal called it a serious matter under the school's safety policy, and the class teacher spoke to the group's members and their parents.
Most of the posts are gone now. I'm okay. Better than last week.
Ojas

qa.q: What did Ma and Baba file on the cybercrime portal?
qa.a: A complaint, with Ojas reading out the dates.

qa.q: How did Ojas feel on Monday, and a week later?
qa.a: Ojas felt sick and scared on Monday, and a week later feels okay and relieved, since most posts are gone.

qa.q: What else could Ojas do now that the posts are mostly gone?
qa.a: Keep in touch with the class teacher and tell Ma and Baba if any copy reappears, so it can be reported again quickly.

qa.q: How might Tarun feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Tarun may be upset for Ojas but glad to hear it directly, and relieved that adults acted the same night.

grounding: Shows a family reporting a fake image to the app, filing a cybercrime complaint, and the school acting under its safety policy.
